channel.title: ResearchBuzz - Transformed
channel.description: News and resources covering social media, search engines, databases, archives, and other such information collections. Since 1998.

item.title: Wooden architecture of the borderlands: new online collection makes the latest knowledge on cultural heritage protection available
item.description: From Šariš Museum and machine-translated from Slovak: “The results of the international professional conference Wooden Architecture of the Borderland are now available to everyone. The collection brings up-to-date knowledge about sacral and folk architecture, traditional building technologies, monument restoration, museum presentation and new approaches to the protection of wooden buildings in the Slovak-Polish border region. It is intended not only for experts, but also for all those interested in the cultural heritage of our regions.”

item.title: LQ’s New Digital Archive Is Now Open
item.description: Lapham’s Quarterly: “With an annual subscription to the Lapham’s Quarterly Substack, you can now read, search, and browse—on a desktop, laptop, tablet, or phone—every issue of Lapham’s Quarterly by logging into our new digital archive, which resides at archive.laphamsquarterly.org.”

item.title: DIY archivists push budget Nikons to 902,000 clicks to save 1,800 rare books — team trains neural net on Photoshop edits to process 526,000 scans
item.description: New-to-me, from Tom’s Hardware: “Around 2015, a trio of Pakistani friends took it upon themselves to digitize a large number of out-of-print books in Urdu, many of them lithographs — they call it the Ibteda Digital Library. They did it for the love of the language, with no budget or support, but after 576,000 shutter counts on a D5300 camera, 326,000 on a D3300, and 526,000 dual-page photos, they have now had to call it quits after a decade.”

item.title: Newly-Available Archival Accessions, April 1-June 30, 2026
item.description: Library of Virginia: “We hold more than 200 million manuscript items, digital images, and records in our archives that tell countless stories of Virginians and our collective past. In addition to state and local government records, the Library has an unparalleled collection of private papers that includes records of businesses, organizations, churches, and individuals. These archival collections continue to grow, and archivists are constantly acquiring and processing records to make them accessible to the public. Four times a year, we publish reports of newly accessioned records. View the New Archival Accession Reports online.”

item.title: LibreOffice 26.8 is out – local first, and with no AI
item.description: The Register: “We do like some of the sly notes in the launch materials, though, starting with the headline: ‘LibreOffice 26.8 brings professional typography, deeper support for the world’s writing systems, and no artificial intelligence'”

item.title: Google TV Streamer gets $50 price increase
item.description: 9to5 Google: “Google has quietly raised the price of the Google TV Streamer to $149.99. This $50 increase is quite drastic for the 2024 Google TV device that launched at $99.99 and saw $20 discounts during the holidays. This new price is already live on the Google Store and Best Buy, but other retailers (like Amazon) are still selling it at the original price as of Monday afternoon.”

item.title: Roblox is cracking down on games that reward kids for doomscrolling
item.description: TechSpot: “After going viral and attracting around half a million concurrent players, the Roblox experience ‘Steal an Egg’ is now facing brand-new restrictions. The widely popular user-generated gaming platform is prohibiting younger players from accessing SAE and similar experiences because they are supposedly designed to encourage kids to watch endless streams of media content through reward-based gameplay mechanics.”

item.title: Florida orders Flock cameras off of state roads
item.description: Orlando Sentinel: “Florida is revoking permits for Flock cameras and similar license-plate readers on state roads, dealing a blow to local law enforcement agencies that say they’re a critical crime-fighting tool. In a memorandum Monday, Florida Department of Transportation Assistant Secretary Will Watts gave agencies 30 days to remove the cameras from state roads, or FDOT will remove them itself.”

item.title: Descendants of enslaved potter David Drake work to reclaim ancestor’s art
item.description: PBS News Hour: “The descendants David Drake, known as Dave the Potter, have traced their lineage back to the once-enslaved potter and launched an effort to reclaim his work. So far, the family has recovered six pieces of Drake’s highly valued glazed stoneware, and they’re working with museums to bring even more back into the family’s hands. They say the effort has not only reconnected them with their family’s legacy, but also raised broader questions about art ownership and restitution.”

item.title: “Horrendous”: MAGA Shreds Trump for Cruel Post on Data Center Critics
item.description: New Republic: “‘I regret ever supporting you.’ ‘You have lost your mind.’ ‘Horrendous messaging.’ These are just a few of the messages that President Trump’s supporters have sent him on Truth Social after his Monday morning attack on opponents of data centers. Trump had defended data center projects, saying communities who oppose them ‘want to end up being backwards and poor.'”

item.title: U.S. gas power proposals tied to data centers nearly doubled in the first half of 2026
item.description: Global Energy Monitor: “The Global Oil and Gas Plant Tracker² now counts 189 gigawatts (GW) of gas-fired capacity in the U.S. across the announced, pre-construction, and construction phases, which is intended to meet the exponential increase in electricity demand brought by the booming data center expansion.”

item.title: AI surveillance in schools raises safety and equity concerns
item.description: Brookings Institution: “In some American schools, administrators have installed bathroom monitoring devices that capture audio to listen for signs of distress. As one Forbes article reports, Motorola, which manufactures the listening devices, claims that the devices only flag sounds of concern in real time, such as gunshots or calls for help, and do not store recorded audio. However, one student was able to hack his school’s device and turn it into a real-time audio eavesdropping bug, disable its detection capabilities, and create fake alerts for gunshots.”

item.title: Pennsylvania’s A.I. Gold Rush Meets Second Thoughts
item.description: New York Times: This link goes to a gift article. “A national backlash against the rapid build-out of data centers has made them a top issue in this fall’s midterm elections. The governor, a potential 2028 presidential candidate, two weeks ago labeled data center developers “predatory” and signed an executive order for what he described as ‘the nation’s strictest guardrails’ for the facilities. He said the state would no longer speed approvals and that data centers must meet new requirements and be approved first by local communities before advancing.”

item.title: The Pentagon now has its own version of ChatGPT and Grok
item.description: TechCrunch: “The Pentagon has launched versions of OpenAI’s ChatGPT and xAI’s Grok, giving 3 million civilian and military personnel access to generative AI tools that have been tailored to ‘warfighter needs.'”

item.title: Sam Altman called Gavin Newsom over kids’ chatbot safety bill
item.description: Politico: “That’s according to four people familiar with details of Altman’s behind-the-scenes maneuvering — including one person with direct knowledge and three others directly involved in talks with OpenAI over the bill, SB 1119. They told POLITICO the OpenAI CEO reached out directly to the governor during a final burst of negotiations last week before the bill passed the state Legislature late Monday night.”

item.title: Gal Gadot Defends Starring in Movie With AI Sets and Lighting Because ‘You’re Going to Work With It or Be Out of the Game’; Lawyers Spent 6 Months Ensuring AI Would Not Alter Actors
item.description: Variety: “Gadot also spoke about her upcoming role in Doug Liman’s ‘Bitcoin,’ which has garnered controversy for using AI to create the movie’s sets and lighting. The cast, which includes Gadot opposite Casey Affleck, Pete Davidson, and Isla Fisher, was shot in a completely barebones space. The film’s producer, Ryan Kavanaugh, has claimed the $70 million production saved more than $200 million by using AI to fill in the production design and lighting.”

item.title: As That Whole ‘Tilly Norwood’ Thing Peters Out, AI Acting Achieves Unsettling Ubiquity on Chinese Phone Screens
item.description: Gizmodo: “Unless there’s a large, secret fandom waiting with bated breath for the release of the Tilly Norwood movie, it would seem that improv comedian Eline Van Der Velden’s quest for fame as an AI provocateur is finally fizzling. But make no mistake: the aesthetic cataclysm Tilly Norwood seemed to prophesy appears to have been real all along. You just have to look at China to see the warning lights flashing.”

item.title: Hollywood studios have sued over AI. Now Google is courting them to use its tools
item.description: Los Angeles Times: “Google executives have approached representatives at Disney, Universal, Warner Bros. Discovery and other studios about licensing intellectual property to be used in AI models, according to three people familiar with the conversations who were not authorized to speak publicly about them. Nonetheless, no agreements have been reached yet, partly because of the complexities of the issues surrounding AI, as well as sensitivities around how Hollywood talent and unions would react, the sources said.”

item.title: Anthropic warns infostealer malware is hijacking Claude sessions to drain usage
item.description: Bleeping Computer: “Anthropic is warning some Claude users that infostealer malware on their PCs has stolen active Claude login sessions, allowing attackers to access accounts and consume their usage. The company is signing affected users out of Claude, removing saved payment methods, and refunding charges it identifies as unauthorized.”

item.title: New Tool Uses AI to Help Undergraduates Think Critically About Research
item.description: North Carolina State University: “An interdisciplinary team of researchers has developed and demonstrated a step-by-step framework called Socratic Challenger that uses artificial intelligence to help undergraduate students cultivate critical thinking skills. Specifically, the framework uses AI as a collaborator to develop research questions that can be pursued in laboratory or classroom settings.”

item.title: 41% of surveyed Australian teens now get their news from AI: new research
item.description: The Conversation: “Since 2017, we have been tracking young people’s media engagement, to understand how they get their news. This time, we found some young people are bypassing traditional outlets, reducing their use of social media sources and getting their news from artificial intelligence (AI) summaries using platforms such as Google search and tools like ChatGPT.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: We have completed the project of digitizing the collections of the Zamość Museum in cooperation with the POLIN Museum of the History of Polish Jews
item.description: From Zamość Museum and machine-translated from Polish: “Recently, the Zamość Museum hosted specialists from the POLIN Museum of the History of Polish Jews – Monika Bondarew and Iwo Książek – who supported the digitization of the museum’s collections. The meeting provided an opportunity not only to conduct work related to the digital development of the collections but also to exchange experiences and knowledge on modern methods of documenting and sharing cultural heritage.”

item.title: is now open!
item.description: Voting for the 2026 Tiny Awards From the FAQ: “Basically what we’re trying to celebrate is people making things on the web for themselves, for the fun of it, for the hell of it, using their imaginations and whatever development tools and processes are available to them. It it interesting? Is it funny? Is it weird? Is it emotive? Is it heartbreaking? Does it make your soul sing? That’s what we want to celebrate!”

item.title: Google AI Overviews Pushing Searchers Into AI Mode, Drops Show More Button
item.description: Search Engine Roundtable: Bleh. “Google Search has confirmed it is now pushing searchers into AI Mode from the AI Overview by default, without having to click the ‘Show more’ button. The new AI Overview experience that Google is testing shows a much fuller AI answer, like you’d get in AI Mode, and loads the follow up ‘Ask anything’ box by default.”

item.title: MapQuest Tops App Store Charts After Refusing ‘Lake America’ Change
item.description: MacRumors: “MapQuest is in the spotlight this week after refusing to change ‘Lake Ontario’ to ‘Lake America’ on its map following an executive order issued by U.S. President Donald Trump last week. As of Monday morning, the MapQuest app is the top free iPhone app on Apple’s App Store charts in Canada and fourth on the equivalent U.S. chart.”

item.title: Meta removes ads for fraud apps posing as porn after India sounds alarm
item.description: Reuters: “Meta on Monday removed dozens of advertisements after India flagged a pattern of Facebook ‌and Instagram ads using sexually explicit content to lure users into downloading malware that could steal banking credentials and drain bank accounts.”

item.title: Hagley Acquires Business Records of New York City Tailor
item.description: Hagley Museum: “Hagley Library recently acquired the Kozinn + Sons Merchant Tailors records, now open for research thanks to archival processing intern Darby Ronning. For over a century, Kozinn + Sons was a New York City–based tailored clothing company led by three generations of the Kozinn family. Kozinn FamilyFounded in 1913 as the Independent Trouser Company, for much of its history the company operated under the name Saunt Lurie Limited.”

item.title: Rice archive of the unexplained gets its own TV series
item.description: Rice University: “More than a million documents, recordings and files on telepathy, near-death experiences and alien encounters have been sitting in a climate-controlled facility outside Houston for years. Starting Oct. 1, they go on national television. ‘Archive X: Unexplained Phenomena,’ a six-part documentary series filmed at Rice University, premieres Oct. 1 at 9 p.m. on SundanceTV, AMC+ and All Reality with new episodes weekly through Nov. 5.”

item.title: The Pentagon Secretly Hires Conservative Influencers To Amplify Pete Hegseth’s Agenda
item.description: Mediaite: “The Pentagon has secretly hired military veterans with massive online followings to act as conservative influencers who can disseminate Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s warrior agenda to the masses. The Washington Post reported Sunday that although these influencers have been placed in government and some civilian roles, the Pentagon refuses to give details on their assignments, ‘despite the Trump administration’s claims that they are running the most transparent Defense Department ever.'”

item.title: Cambodia claims it has wiped out online scam compounds after a sweeping crackdown
item.description: Associated Press: “Cambodia, notorious for being a major center for international online scams, claimed Friday it no longer hosts any of the compounds where the lucrative cybercrime was carried out, although some remain skeptical.”

item.title: New York Nightclub Threatens to Permanently Ban Anyone Caught With Smart Glasses
item.description: PetaPixel: “As Futurism reports, Basement in Queens, New York, is an underground techno club that has become one of the city’s best-known spots. It models itself on nightclubs in Europe, such as Berlin’s Berghain, operating a strict door policy where revelers have to pass the ‘vibe check.’ But it appears that smart glasses definitely don’t pass the vibe check, as in a statement posted to the club’s Instagram account yesterday, the club made its stance clear.”

item.title: W&M professor awarded NEH grant to manage Yorktown archaeological collections
item.description: William & Mary: “Every artifact tells a story, but without careful preservation, those stories can fade with time. In William & Mary anthropology department, Assistant Teaching Professor Kimberley Connor is cataloging and and digitizing archaeological collections from Yorktown and their associates, preserving their stories and making them more accessible for generations to come.”

item.title: We Are Living in the Fantasy World of 13-Year-Old Boys
item.description: The Atlantic: “What stayed with the Silicon Valley magnates was the idea of abandoning our bodies and the messiness of other people, leaving behind our finitude for an infinity of stars and self-coding machines. But this is actually a nightmare, a false escape, as the source material hints at without much subtlety. What happens next may depend on whether these boys grow up and finally recognize what they failed to see before.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: Paraguay Launches Digital Archive Of 19th And 20th Century History
item.description: The Asunción Times: “Paraguay has launched a new digital platform providing public access to nearly 100,000 pages of historical documents and newspapers. The digital archive, titled “Memoria escrita de un Gigante 1845-1904” (Written Memory of a Giant 1845-1904), was presented by the Ministry of Education and Sciences (MEC).”

item.title: Google’s August 2026 spam update hit rankings harder than normal
item.description: Search Engine Land: “Google’s spam update caused exceptional search disruption, with dramatic ranking losses across 20 industries, according to SE Ranking data. Google’s August 2026 spam update saw an 82% increase in top 10 URLs dropping out of the top 100 compared with a period without a confirmed ranking update, according to new SE Ranking data.”

item.title: Google made a cozy mobile game called ‘Froggy’s World’ & the whimsy is back
item.description: 9to5 Google: “Google has quietly released a cozy mobile game called Froggy’s World in the vein of Animal Crossing and Stardew Valley. Froggy’s World is accessed by searching ‘weather’ on Google Search and tapping the new ‘play’ icon in the top-right corner of the Knowledge Panel card.”

item.title: As Bluesky adds more videos, YouTube adds more Bluesky-style custom feeds
item.description: Tubefilter: “YouTube is factoring user preferences into its video recommendations. Earlier this year, the video hub launched an experiment centered around ‘custom feeds’ — landing pages unified by a specific topic, focus, or vibe. Now, YouTube is expanding its ongoing test by letting users set up multiple custom feeds on a single account.”

item.title: Judge in Google privacy class action awards lawyers $147 million in legal fees
item.description: Reuters: “A U.S. judge on Friday awarded nearly $147 million in legal fees to plaintiffs’ lawyers who won a $425 million jury verdict against Alphabet’s Google in a data privacy ​trial last year, while denying the company’s bid for an order rejecting the ‌jury’s verdict.”

item.title: Privacy watchdog takes Google to court over ‘right to be forgotten’ case
item.description: Global News: “Canada’s privacy commissioner is asking the Federal Court to order Google to de-list specific search results, after Google refused to comply with the watchdog’s recommendations. The privacy commissioner’s office said a year ago that Google wouldn’t implement its recommendation to de-list specific articles in the search results for an individual’s name.”

item.title: Culture and ethics meets tech: UCLA debuts country’s first bachelor’s in digital humanities
item.description: Associated Press: “UCLA is launching the nation’s first digital humanities department and bachelor’s degree this fall. The new discipline combines classical humanities with technical know-how to examine a digitized and increasingly AI-enhanced world.”

item.title: Three Years, Thousands of Fish and a Labor of Love to Preserve Them All
item.description: Buffalo Museum of Science: “Her work on the three-year-long, federally funded project enabled the Museum to fully catalog and properly preserve all of the fish specimens in the fluid collection. At the heart of the collection, Abbey [Hines] and her team preserved 1,173 jars of fish specimens inherited from the Hadley Collection. About 1,100 had not been properly sorted.”

item.title: Charkha, century-old charpai: Punjab village boy turns small room at home into museum
item.description: The Tribune (India): “A charkha (spinning wheel), a century-old charpai (a form of bed predominantly used in rural areas) and age-old coins are some of the contents that can be found in a room at Harnampura village in Sahnewal. The room belongs to Harman, a BA final-year student at a college in Doraha. He has saved more than 200 rare objects from pre-Partition Punjab and turned his room into a museum.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: New database to support users in navigating over 2000 biodiversity portals, platforms and tools
item.description: UNEP-WCMC: “To better communicate the uses of existing data systems, scientists at UNEP-WCMC have developed a new database of 698 global, more than 200 regional and 1,400 national online biodiversity data systems. They have also created a new typology to categorize these systems, which will help users navigate existing datasets and better select ones relevant to their needs.”

item.title: Hoover Institution Launches California Decides
item.description: Hoover Institution: “The Hoover Institution today announced the launch of California Decides, a new civic education initiative designed to give Californians clear, accessible, and evidence-based information about how their state works, the policy challenges it faces, and the choices voters will make at the ballot box. Launching ahead of the November 2026 election, California Decides will examine issues including housing affordability, energy, education, public safety, state finances, election administration, regulation, and government reform.”

item.title: Key witness in Meta trial says terms of settlement insufficient to halt apps’ harms to teenagers
item.description: The Guardian: “The star witness in the US government’s landmark trial against Meta believes that a multibillion-dollar settlement reached on Wednesday does not go far enough to stop the social media giant’s harms to young users. ‘The limitations that are in the agreement are the equivalent of saying: “Well, you can smoke as many cigarettes as you can in two hours a day,”‘ said whistleblower and ex-Facebook employee Arturo Béjar. ‘It doesn’t make the cigarettes any safer.'”

item.title: Google changes spam policy in EU to avert antitrust fine
item.description: Reuters: “The EU said ​that its monitoring showed that Google’s spam policy demoted news media ​and other publishers’ websites and content in Google search results, when those websites include content from commercial partners. Google said that from August 30 any manual actions ​taken to demote sites would not apply to users in ​the 27 EU nations, Iceland, Norway and Liechtenstein (the European Economic Area).”

item.title: Stars and Stripes journalists facing firing get one-week reprieve
item.description: Politico: “The Pentagon gave a one-week reprieve Friday to three staff members at Stars and Stripes facing imminent dismissal for speaking out about threats to editorial independence at a military news outlet that receives partial government funding. The delay was announced during a hastily-called hearing Friday in federal court in Washington on a lawsuit filed a day earlier by reporter Lara Korte, editor-in-chief Erik Slavin, and publisher Max Lederer.”

item.title: Influencers Have a Lot to Say About Politics. Many Are Quietly Paid for It.
item.description: New York Times: This link goes to a gift article. Also, I don’t take a damn dime from anybody to shill anything, including people and ideologies. “There are no federal regulations requiring disclosure of payments for political support on social media, and only a few states have such rules. That allows influencers, in most instances, to endorse candidates for a fee without ever disclosing those payments in their posts. Creators say some campaigns have even asked them to actively conceal the fact that they’re being compensated, making it impossible to know what’s genuine support — and what is pay-for-play.”

item.title: CISA confirms hackers targeted over 100 US water systems during July
item.description: TechCrunch: “U.S. cybersecurity agency CISA said it has observed cyberattacks targeting over 100 internet-exposed systems across the U.S. water and wastewater sector, amid a wave of hacks targeting American critical infrastructure. The number of affected systems provides new context to the scale of the ongoing cyberattacks targeting water providers in Michigan, Minnesota, and at least five other states.”

item.title: Influencer pleads guilty to criminal impersonation for viral pranks at Arizona businesses
item.description: Associated Press: “A social media influencer known for posting viral videos of pranks has pleaded guilty to criminal impersonation in Arizona for posing as an employee of businesses in a Phoenix suburb and orchestrating brief but chaotic takeover attempts…. Heston James Cobb, who posts as ‘Heston James,’ was arrested in July 2025 after police in Tempe say he and others went into businesses posing as workers, entered employee-only areas and refused to leave when asked to do so.”

item.title: ‘Heritage Forensics’ investigates cultural heritage caught up in war
item.description: Cornell University: “In ‘Heritage Forensics: Culture on the Front Lines of the Armenia-Azerbaijan Conflict,’ CHW researchers including Lori Khatchadourian, professor of Near Eastern studies and anthropology in the College of Arts and Sciences (A&S) and Adam T. Smith, the Henry Scarborough Professor of Social Science in anthropology (A&S), describe their new framework for studying cultural heritage in war zones, drawing on the investigative reports of the Nagorno-Karabakh wars CHW released between 2021 and 2025.”

item.title: Ceuta migration sparks nearly 9,600 hate posts on social media
item.description: Euronews: “The Spanish Observatory on Racism and Xenophobia logged 9,590 hate messages in two days tied to a July influx of some 80,000 migrants into Ceuta. The latest incident in Ceuta sent hate speech on social media soaring, with 9,590 posts detected by the Spanish Observatory on Racism and Xenophobia (OBERAXE) in just two days, coinciding with the mass arrival of migrants on 30 and 31 July, which the government put at around 80,000 people.”

item.title: Social media: Reading between the lines
item.description: UC Irvine: “Researchers analyzed 24,598 heat-related posts on Twitter, now X, from across California between 2016 and 2022. They found that where people live, how they get around and the resources available to them were associated with meaningful differences in how they talked about extreme heat – including whether they described its effects on their lives or discussed ways of coping with it.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: Kansas town drops charges against teacher arrested for clapping during public hearings on data centers — says that ‘case has been dismissed without prejudice’
item.description: Tom’s Hardware: “Lux Claridge, the teacher who was arrested in Emporia, Kansas, during an AI data center meeting for clapping, said that the city has dropped the charges against them. According to 404 Media, the Emporia assistant city attorney told Claridge’s lawyer that the case has been dismissed without prejudice in municipal court because of conflicts on the matter. Unfortunately, that doesn’t mean that they’re in the clear yet, as the case has been bumped to the County Attorney’s office for further review.”

item.title: US datacenters tripled their water footprint in 10 years
item.description: The Register: “Datacenters in America used about 17 billion gallons of water during 2023, triple the amount they used a decade earlier in 2014, according to an estimate from US Congressional Research Service (CRS).”

item.title: Unlikely Winners of the Data Center Boom: Sound Consultants
item.description: Bloomberg: “Acoustic consultants, whose once-niche profession focuses on solving issues around noise and vibration, have suddenly found themselves in high demand thanks to the rapid development of data centers, an inherently noisy business. Developers are hiring them in droves to survey the ambient sound levels near facility boundaries to guide the noise limits set by local governments and to proactively defend themselves against community blowback from neighbors. Some nearby homeowners argue, however, that builders are seeking to capture artificially inflated readings, so they’re in turn hiring their own sound experts to conduct competing assessments — all of which adds up to boom times for the acoustic professionals.”

item.title: OpenAI to end model access to Cursor after acquisition by Elon Musk’s SpaceX
item.description: CNBC: “OpenAI announced late Friday that it is ending developers’ access to its models on Cursor, following the acquisition of the AI coding startup by Elon Musk’s SpaceX earlier this month.”

item.title: AI agents are all the rage—but research shows they leak private data
item.description: Wake Forest University: “Ying Zhang, an assistant professor in Wake Forest University’s Department of Computer Science, studies security in software engineering. Her latest research, ‘How Your Credentials Are Leaked by LLM Agent Skills,’ explores how large language model (LLM) agents make data vulnerable to attacks.”

item.title: New Mexico judges working on statewide guidelines for artificial intelligence use in court
item.description: Source New Mexico: “Second Judicial District Family Court Judge Jane Levy and Sixth Judicial District Judge Jarod Hofacket spoke before the interim Courts, Corrections and Justice Committee in Albuquerque on Tuesday and updated them on their AI-focused efforts. They said they are working on three separate sets of guidelines — one each for self-representing litigants, attorneys and judicial staff.”

item.title: Musicians-turned-detectives are hunting for AI grifters
item.description: The Verge: “For musicians — especially those creating art in technologically-focused spaces like electronic dance music — the increasingly complicated question of what is ‘real’ and what isn’t feels particularly urgent and personal. Professional courtesy can make this only more complex; listeners can call out performers they suspect of using gen AI, but it’s something else for artists to raise concerns about their professional peers. There are some though, like 26-year-old EDM producer Max ‘H4RRIS’ Harris, who are taking a stand against generative technology with videos calling out anyone they believe is trying to pass off AI slop as human-made art.”

item.title: Should the Press ‘Run Toward’ AI?
item.description: Columbia Journalism Review: “The Washington Post (Ask the Post AI) and Financial Times (Ask FT) have made chatbots from their journalism, and Jim VandeHei, the cofounder and CEO of Axios, talked to Issie Lapowsky for a recent CJR story about Axios’s partnership with OpenAI and what he views as its potential to ‘save local news.’ Many big publishers are cutting licensing deals with tech firms. But the idea of embracing AI is harder to swallow for others.”

item.title: Anthropic is cutting Claude Code’s current weekly limits by 17%
item.description: Bleeping Computer: “Anthropic is permanently increasing Claude Code’s standard weekly usage limits by 25% for Pro, Max, Team, and seat-based Enterprise plans, but it’s not as good as it sounds. If you use Claude, you’re actually getting a 17% reduction compared to what you have today.”

item.title: Are you a ‘meat proxy’? The latest AI slang, explained.
item.description: Mashable: “There is a new name for the coworker who responds to a simple question with seven paragraphs that very clearly came straight from ChatGPT: a ‘meat proxy.’ You probably know the type. They paste a question into an AI chatbot, copy the answer into Slack, and consider their work complete. The response may be long, polished, and packed with suspiciously corporate phrases, but it contains very little evidence that the person sending it has actually read it.”

item.title: Now Sony Music Publishing and Warner Chappell sue Anthropic in multi-billion dollar lawsuit: ‘One of the largest and most blatant ongoing thefts of intellectual property in history.’
item.description: Music Business Worldwide: “Sony Music Publishing and Warner Chappell Music have joined forces to sue Anthropic, home of Claude, over what the publishers call ‘one of the largest and most blatant ongoing thefts of intellectual property in history.'”

item.title: Gibraltar faces data center developer lawsuit after city passes moratorium
item.description: Planet Detroit: “The developers of a proposed 100-megawatt data center on the former McLouth Steel property in Gibraltar are suing the city over its one-year data center moratorium.”

item.title: After Experiment, Journal Decides to Prohibit AI-Authored Content
item.description: Daily Nous: “Earlier this month, the journal Philosophy & Public Affairs published an article largely written by an AI. The article was described as an experiment by the philosopher who submitted it, Simon Goldstein (Hong Kong), and its publication was similarly described by the journal’s editor in chief, Jason Brennan (Georgetown). Now that the experiment has been discussed a fair amount here and elsewhere online, the journal has decided from now on to prohibit AI-authored content.”

item.title: What AI can tell us about California redwoods and fog
item.description: Northern Arizona University: “California’s redwood forests are a national treasure. And the coastal fog that often covers the trees in a mysterious gray shroud? That’s no less beloved. A few researchers at NAU believe those trees, and that fog, are worth protecting. So they’re using machine learning to investigate how the two work together to create a healthy, resilient forest—and how less fog due to climate change may spell trouble for redwood trees in the coming decades.” Good evening, Internet…

item.title: Child advocacy group launches ‘living resource’ for childhood well-being data
item.description: Alabama Reflector: “Alabama’s leading source of children’s well-being data and research plans to launch a new online data center to increase access to up-to-date information, the group announced Wednesday. VOICES for Alabama’s Children, a nonprofit organization, is moving its annual research project to an online dashboard that can be updated as new data becomes available, becoming a ‘living resource.'”

item.title: Buddy Icon Archive
item.description: Found in my Calishat Snaps: From the site’s short history of AIM buddy icons: “The canvas was so small that every decision became emphatic. Surviving client documentation describes images between 48×48 and 50×50 pixels. A face needed a close crop; text needed blunt contrast; an idea often had to survive in a single glance. Animated GIFs turned that square into a tiny cinematic form. A 2003 essay about BadassBuddy noticed camera movement, cuts, lighting, and short narratives squeezed into the icon window. Some loops lasted only a few seconds. That was enough time for a reaction, a punch line, a declaration of love, or a cartoon character to suffer a compact but complete misfortune.”

item.title: Meta Doesn’t Want to Be a Social Media Company Anymore
item.description: Mother Jones: “Like virtually every other tech company, then, Meta executives have turned from social media as their core product, to a gauzy, pie-eyed future of AI as the future of work, business and everything else. Laws, legislation and jury settlements are often backwards-looking when it comes to tech companies. This particular settlement attempts to mitigate the harm of their current products, while companies like Meta are already focused, for better or much more likely worse, on what’s next.”

item.title: ‘Thin Air,’ Real Money: Donald Trump’s Crypto Products Have Left Investors at Least $4.7 Billion Underwater
item.description: Public Citizen: “According to Public Citizen’s analysis, Trump’s crypto schemes have left investors at least an estimated $4.7 billion underwater. These losses are largely unrealized and, in the case of his meme coin, reflect wealth transferred to a small group of early buyers rather than money that simply vanished.”

item.title: To Silicon Valley, anything could be a ‘psyop’
item.description: CNN: “Most Americans don’t want AI data centers near them. There are plenty of well-reported reasons why: People may be concerned about the environmental impacts, or angry over AI companies threatening mass unemployment and skeptical of promises that data centers will usher in a jobs boom. They could be worried about higher utility bills. Then there’s the noise. The constant, maddening noise. But in Silicon Valley, a different, more sinister explanation for the anti-data center movement has taken hold.”

item.title: Flipboard acquires Graze, the feed builder working to monetize the open social web
item.description: TechCrunch: “Flipboard, the news magazine software company that has more recently invested in the open social web — the umbrella term for social platforms that let users, not one company, control their own data and audience — is making another big bet on that ecosystem. The company on Wednesday announced it’s acquiring the Portland-based feed-building startup Graze, which has been working to monetize the open social web by allowing feed creators to support themselves via ads.”

item.title: Three UK airports hit by cyber-attack with data of 8.7m customers accessed
item.description: The Guardian: “Manchester, London Stansted and East Midlands airports have been hit by a cyber-attack in which hackers accessed the data of about 8.7 million customers.”

item.title: Speed Art Museum begins repatriation of 24 Native American cultural items
item.description: Spectrum News: “The Speed Art Museum is returning 24 cultural items to the Southern Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes as part of a federal repatriation process under the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act.”

item.title: Creating an Open-source Blogging Studies Syllabus
item.description: Brennan.Day: “The premise for this is rather simple: I am going to create a static site that will act as the syllabus and curriculum for Blogging Studies, and it will include lessons/lectures, assignments, recommended readings, and methods for class participation. Blogging Studies is a term I coined myself, and I define it as the study and practice of writing craft and independent online publishing as a single, integrated discipline, treating the blog post medium as a legitimate unit of scholarly and creative work.”

item.title: An otter, a beaver — and now a mink spotted in the Bronx
item.description: Gothamist: “A week after announcing his camera trap had captured the first otter in the Bronx River in a century, a local wildlife researcher was surprised to see a new face in his lens: an American mink.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: Data For Dummies: Hawaiʻi Facts For Those Of Us Who Can’t Read Spreadsheets
item.description: Honolulu Civil Beat: “Now that another primary election has come and gone, I’ve been wondering: Is Hawaiʻi still the worst in the nation when it comes to voter turnout? Fortunately, the folks who built Hawaiʻi Dashboard, a cool new database of key Hawaiʻi facts, figures and trends, were reading my mind.”

item.title: Ministry for Foreign Affairs makes Raoul Wallenberg documents available in new database
item.description: Government Offices of Sweden: “On Raoul Wallenberg Day, 27 August, the Ministry for Foreign Affairs is presenting a new digital database containing the documents in the Raoul Wallenberg case preserved in the Ministry’s archives. The collection comprises documents from the period 1945–2018, approximately 71 000 pages in several languages, and provides researchers, journalists and the public with online access to material that sheds light on both Mr Wallenberg’s efforts during the Second World War and the long-standing efforts to clarify his fate.”

item.title: [Exclusive] Google builds Korea team for full-functioning Maps service
item.description: Korea Herald: “Google is stepping up preparations to expand Google Maps in South Korea by recruiting a senior partnerships manager, as the company says it is ‘officially launching full-functioning Google Maps capabilities’ in the country.”

item.title: Judge dismisses lawsuit by Elon Musk’s X challenging New York hate speech law
item.description: Reuters: “A U.S. judge on Wednesday dismissed a lawsuit by Elon Musk’s ​X seeking to void a New York state law requiring social media ‌companies to disclose how they monitor hate speech, extremism, harassment, foreign political interference and disinformation.”

item.title: White House teleprompter operator ordered to pay $172K for placing prediction market bets on Trump’s speeches
item.description: NBC News: “A teleprompter operator for President Donald Trump who made online prediction trades based on information from upcoming speeches has been ordered to pay $172,000, a federal agency said Friday night. Gabriel Perez used ‘material, nonpublic information’ he obtained through his job to place ‘trades’ on a prediction market, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission said in a news release.”

item.title: Google Search Showing Fewer PDF Files. But Why?
item.description: Search Engine Roundtable: “Google seems to be showing fewer and fewer PDF files, and when it does show PDF files, it seems not to show them from some pretty important sites, like IRS.gov, New York State, and some others. But in some cases we are seeing Google show PDF documents, without you having to explicitly filter for PDF file types.”

item.title: What’s hot on TikTok LIVE? You can find out through a new newsletter.
item.description: Tubefilter: “TikTok has a plan to make live streaming less intimidating for new users, and that plan involves Substack. The media platform is the home of The Creator’s Cut, a newsletter that shares tips and best practices related to TikTok LIVE.”

item.title: Gov. Abbott blocks state agencies from spending money on Flock cameras
item.description: Texas Tribune: “Gov. Greg Abbott has ordered all state agencies to pause funding for Flock cameras as scrutiny over the AI-powered surveillance devices has mounted. The order came as The Texas Tribune was preparing to publish an investigation detailing how a state agency has devoted at least $30 million to building up the state’s Flock surveillance network by providing grants to local police departments.”

item.title: Prediction Markets Should Be Regulated as Gambling, Appeals Court Says
item.description: New York Times: This link goes to a gift article. “A federal appeals court ruled on Friday that states had the ability to regulate prediction markets, a win for the states in an ongoing battle with federal regulators over who had authority over popular wagering platforms. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit in San Francisco rejected Kalshi’s request for relief against Nevada’s gambling laws, after the state sued the company in February for ‘unlicensed operations.'”

item.title: Info for confidential voters was made public in Colorado secretary of state web update, office confirms
item.description: Denver Post: “The Colorado Secretary of State’s Office made information for more than 130,000 confidential voters publicly accessible for over a week because of an error in updating a voter registration tool, agency officials said Thursday. Agency staff confirmed that 59 voter profiles for people who had requested that their records not be publicly disclosed were accessed between Aug. 14 and late Tuesday afternoon, when the problem was discovered.”

item.title: Belize Establishes First National Music Archive
item.description: San Pedro Sun: “Belize officially marked a major step in preserving its cultural heritage on August 24th, when Honorable Francis Fonseca, Minister of Culture, announced the establishment of the country’s first Belize Music Archive and the National Recording Treasures of Belize. The initiative was launched through the Belize Music Project, with a new archive laboratory opened at the Belize Archives and Records Service in Belmopan.”

item.title: Mapping the Survivors: Rene Ligon’s Quest to Document the World’s Remaining Douglas DC-3s
item.description: Vintage Aviation News: “What began as a search for airworthy Douglas DC-3s to photograph has grown into a worldwide research project. Aviation photographer Rene Ligon has documented nearly 600 surviving airframes—from working transports and museum exhibits to forgotten wrecks in remote locations.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: The 14,000 followers of ‘Historic Boston Archives’ are calling out its insane AI videos
item.description: Boston.com: “Whoever runs the Facebook page ‘Historical Boston Archives’ probably didn’t think they were fooling anybody when they posted old photos of Boston brought to life on video — they probably just thought they looked cool. But that hasn’t stopped many of its 14,000 followers from calling the posts out as ‘AI slop,’ some of them in hilarious fashion.”

item.title: Photos of ‘Cat in the Hat Serial Killer’ Are AI-Generated, Police Say
item.description: PetaPixel: “AI-generated pictures and videos purporting to show one of Dr. Seuss’ characters as a serial killer have prompted police in the U.K. and Ireland to state that ‘Cat in the Hat was not in your driveway.'”

item.title: More Arkansas communities putting data centers on hold
item.description: Arkansas Times: “The number of Arkansas communities rejecting or imposing new limits on data centers is growing faster than the list of places considering such projects publicly. Madison County joined four other counties in passing a three-year moratorium on data center projects last week, though it doesn’t have any known projects in development. The pause is the second-longest in the state; only Independence County’s is longer.”

item.title: One of East Coast’s largest data centers accused of ‘violating federal law’
item.description: Floodlight: “The largest planned AI data center in New Jersey is being accused of violating federal law after a Floodlight visual investigation found the site running dozens of unpermitted gas-powered generators. Thermal drone footage we captured last week showed the partly completed DataOne facility in Vineland was operating at least 45 of the site’s 62 generators at the time.”

item.title: Blue-collar jobs are the new flashpoint in data-center fight
item.description: Wall Street Journal: “Nationwide resistance to the construction has grown so broad that politicians on both sides of the aisle have halted approvals or tightened oversight as midterm elections approach. Unions and construction trade groups are now entering the fray from the other side, warning that such actions endanger thousands of building-related jobs. They are threatening to withhold support of candidates opposing the data-center projects.”

item.title: Data center developers are pushing Pa. government officials to sign secrecy agreements. At least some are saying yes.
item.description: River Reporter: “Public records requests filed by Spotlight PA found at least eight NDAs signed by township, county, and Shapiro administration officials for data center projects. Why they signed and whether the NDA shaped an eventual deal isn’t always clear. Only two lawmakers who signed such agreements responded to the newsroom’s requests for comment.”

item.title: New state law to protect consumers from data center costs faces its first test
item.description: Florida Trib: “The case before Florida’s Public Service Commission is weighing whether Duke Energy plans to do enough to shield customers from the costs of data centers – probing how state regulators will enforce a law intended to ensure that the energy-intensive facilities and not regular ratepayers are the ones covering the data center costs.”

item.title: Colorado Sen. Cathy Kipp submits first complaint under state’s deepfake disclosure law
item.description: Colorado Newsline: “Sen. Cathy Kipp, a Fort Collins Democrat, filed a complaint with the office on Aug. 5 against the Independence Institute, as first reported by CBS Colorado. She alleges that a video posted to multiple Independence Institute social media accounts violates a 2024 law that requires disclosure on deepfake videos of candidates within 90 days of a general election.”

item.title: ‘It’s high-tech theft’: As AI music booms, Canadian artists demand consent, transparency and pay
item.description: Canadian Press: “Cadence Weapon never gave artificial intelligence permission to learn from his music. But the Edmonton-raised rapper, born Rollie Pemberton, says he recently found 129 of his songs in datasets used to train AI music generators. He was alarmed, but not surprised. To Pemberton, it’s part of a broader fight musicians face as AI-generated music floods streaming platforms and companies train models on existing creative work, often without artists’ knowledge or consent.”

item.title: Museums and AI: Critical Decisions
item.description: American Alliance of Museums: “Welcome to CFM’s summer series on all things Artificial Intelligence. To catch up with our coverage so far, read three scenarios of potential AI futures—bright, dark, and muddling through—commentary by Nik Honeysett on how AI is changing how people encounter information; and a tour of the National Archives Museum’s new AI-powered exhibition. Today I’m sharing my working outline of key decisions museums face about the use of artificial intelligence.”

item.title: Your WordPress.com Site Now Works from Inside ChatGPT
item.description: WordPress: No thanks, I’m good. “You can now manage your WordPress.com site from ChatGPT using the new WordPress.com ChatGPT plugin. Set it up once, then talk to your site to publish posts, moderate comments, check traffic, update media, and handle the small jobs that start after the writing ends.”

item.title: Microsoft AI watermarks in Paint and Photos are linked to user IDs, researcher finds
item.description: The Register: “When Anthropic disclosed earlier this month that it would be applying a statistical word-choice watermark to its Claude text output, the company noted that at least 190 AI providers have agreed to abide by Europe’s AI transparency rules. One such company is Microsoft, which has been applying its own form of watermarking to images created with the assistance of AI in its Paint and Photos applications for Windows.”

item.title: OpenAI Has to Answer to Alabama on Hugging Face Hack
item.description: Gizmodo: “OpenAI’s general attitude towards the fact that one of its AI models went rogue and hacked into the systems of the open-source AI platform Hugging Face has been, ‘That’s our bad, but you gotta admit, it’s pretty cool, right?’ The Attorney General of Alabama’s answer to that is a pretty resounding ‘No.’ On Monday, Alabama AG Steve Marshall announced that he had launched an investigation into the incident and is demanding that OpenAI respond.”

item.title: Study: AI growth requires huge electric grid upgrades
item.description: Columbia Missourian: “A new federal report shows the electric grid across much of the country is strained, requiring thousands of miles of new power lines and billions of dollars in investments. The National Transmission Needs Study shows that approximately 4,000 miles of power lines will need to be replaced each year for the next few decades.”

item.title: SLAC researchers develop AI-based tool to compress data without losing detail
item.description: SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory: “Next-generation science experiments will collect more data than ever – so much so that they’ll surpass the capabilities of current data storage and analysis methods. To help, researchers at the Department of Energy’s SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory developed a method to use artificial intelligence to compress large amounts of raw data without losing subtle details critical to scientific discovery.” Good evening, Internet…

item.title: Ohio launches dashboards tracking education, careers of high school grads
item.description: Spectrum News: “Two new resources are now available for Ohioans to gain an insight into student’s education and workforce outcomes after high school. The Ohio Department of Education and Workforce (DEW) Director Stephen D. Dackin announced the launch of Ohio High School Outcomes and Ohio Career and Technical Education Outcomes.”

item.title: Meta is closing a loophole that allowed people to record with their smart glasses’ light covered
item.description: Engadget: “Meta is making yet another change to its smart glasses to try to prevent people from covertly recording others. The company is rolling out a software update that closes one loophole that allowed people to bypass the LED by covering it up while a recording was in progress, according to Alex Himel, Meta’s VP of AR.”

item.title: Extract and Review Web Page Links Using a Bookmarklet
item.description: Adam’s Desk: “I set out to figure out a solution to extract and then review all web page links using a bookmarklet. I’ve found the bookmarklet I created ‘List Page Links’ to be quite useful and figured I should share it with you dear reader. Come along to discover what are bookmarklets, the advantages of this simple bookmarklet, how to install and run it.”

item.title: Dan Rodricks: Launching from Baltimore, an app connecting musicians by the score
item.description: Baltimore Fishbowl: “Imagine that you’re a musician — cellist, pianist, lead guitar in a rock band, Gospel singer, sax player in a jazz ensemble — and you’re practicing some new piece, or even an old one you never quite mastered. Imagine further that you’re stuck somewhere in the sheet music, that you’re playing adagio when you should be at allegro. Imagine being able to instantly find someone somewhere — anywhere in the world — who’s practicing the same piece at the same time you are.”

item.title: Inside the rise of Maine’s partisan ‘pink slime’ news pages
item.description: Sun-Journal: “The Portland Press Herald identified three recently created sites in Maine with the hallmarks of pink slime on both sides of the partisan aisle: Maine Newsroom, the Portland Post and Maine Policy Updates. The sites differ in partisan orientation, source of funding, and the extent to which any editors or authors can be identified. Each page presents itself as a reputable local news source while posting steady streams of politicized news. They are all run by either super PACs, nationwide dark money groups or partisan operatives, all obscuring their roles in swaying Maine’s media ecosystem for political benefit.”

item.title: IRS Website Drops Heavily In Google Search
item.description: Search Engine Roundtable: “Over the past few days, the IRS website (and other government sites) has tanked within Google’s search results. My gut feeling is that the federal government implemented some bot-blocking that was too aggressive and blocked Google, among others, resulting in Google not fully showing the IRS website. I believe the IRS implemented some fixes, and the website is slowly coming back in Google Search.”

item.title: The German Bundestag has copyright problems
item.description: Heise Online: “Suddenly, a part of the Bundestag’s history is missing: Since April, the online archive for the years 2005 to 2016 is no longer available on the Bundestag website. Content ranging from consultation processes to parliamentary biographies has disappeared: the so-called web archive, with which the content of the respective legislative periods of the parliament was frozen in a kind of space-time continuum at the end of each period and preserved for posterity.”

item.title: Fifth Circuit sides with news aggregator in copyright battle
item.description: Courthouse News Service: “News aggregator NewsBreak prevailed Thursday in a copyright dispute with a publisher who took issue with embedded news articles displayed on NewBreak’s app. Emmerich Newspapers, which publishes local newspapers across Mississippi, Louisiana and Arkansas, had challenged a lower court’s decision that NewsBreak did not violate its copyright.”

item.title: Psychologists Examine Downside of Social Media Algorithms
item.description: University of Texas at Dallas: “While social media algorithms have become excellent at matching a user’s viewing habits with targeted, personalized content, psychologists at The University of Texas at Dallas have determined that these algorithms may have a negative influence on a user’s mental health.”

item.title: How Scholars and Musicians Recreated a Song Lost for More Than 400 Years
item.description: Yale University: “From May 14-16, the group worked to contextualize and recreate the Chorus Brasilicus, a song in Tupi—an Indigenous language of Brazil—that was performed before the king of Portugal and Spain in 1619. The lyrics of this song survived in a text describing the play in which it was performed, but the music did not. The effort culminated in a live performance of the reconstructed work and continued in a workshop at the University of Brasília on May 18.” The music is included with the article. It’s a good listen. Good afternoon, Internet…
